column1: # Cases that run in the PowerShell suite only, and why (#280).
# Read by test-hooks.sh alongside block-dangerous.cases.tsv. A case named here
# counts as accounted for: it is not covered in both dialects, but it is not
# forgotten either. The ratchet then has two numbers instead of one -- cases
# with no counterpart, and cases with no counterpart and no reason.
# Format, tab-separated, three fields:
#   name <TAB> kind <TAB> reason
# The name must match the case name in test-hooks.ps1 exactly. Lines starting
# with '#' and blank lines are ignored.
# Recognised kinds -- an excuse has to fit a shape someone can argue with:
#   policy       the case runs under a declared policy (Set-Policy), and the
#                shared table has no field for one, so a row could only ever
#                assert the default
#   reason-text  the case asserts the wording of the hook's reason, and the
#                shared table records a verdict with no expected-reason field
#   harness      the assertion is not "one payload, one verdict" at all
# Saying why not has to cost something, or it becomes the cheaper option.
# Five guards in test-hooks.sh keep this file honest:
#   1. the name must exist as a real case in test-hooks.ps1, so the gap cannot
#      be closed by excusing cases nobody wrote;
#   2. the kind must be one of the three above;
#   3. the reason must actually say something, so "n/a" cannot stand in;
#   4. a reason for a case the shared table already covers is stale and fails,
#      so a migration cannot leave its excuse behind;
#   5. the number of rows here has its own ceiling, so adding one is a visible,
#      deliberate edit and never a way to quiet a failing ratchet.
# Notably absent is a "PowerShell-only syntax" kind. Every case that once
# claimed it -- Remove-Item, Copy-Item, Start-Process, the call operator --
# was measured against the bash hook in #280, and it reached the identical
# verdict on all nine. The hook classifies a command line as text; being able
# to run the command was never what decided whether a case could be shared.
# If you are about to add a row here because the command is PowerShell, that
# measurement says you are about to add it to the wrong file.
a delete is approved under a declared FS_WRITE=auto
column3: Runs under Set-Policy AUTONOMY_CAT_FS_WRITE=auto; the shared table has no field for a declared policy, so a row could only assert the default ask.

column1: a declared FS_WRITE=auto still cannot lift a hard-deny
column3: The point is that an opt-in does not reach the deny tier, which only a declared policy can express; the shared table has no field for a declared policy.

column1: the same delete asks again once the opt-in is withdrawn
column3: Asserts the effect of withdrawing an opt-in, so it depends on two policy states in order; a row carries neither.

column1: a Databricks job submit is approved under a declared DATABRICKS=auto
column3: Runs under Set-Policy AUTONOMY_CAT_DATABRICKS=auto; the shared table has no field for a declared policy.

column1: a declared DATABRICKS=deny denies what the shipped config never denies
column3: Asserts a verdict the shipped configuration never produces, so the declared policy is the case; the shared table has no field for a declared policy.
